# Cosmogenic dating of glacial moraines

A moraine is dated by the cosmic ray exposure of the boulders sitting on its
crest. The boulders were quarried, transported and dropped by the ice, so their
exposure clock starts the day the glacier retreated and left them at the surface.

## Sampling boulders on the crest

Take five to eight samples per moraine: the largest boulders with a flat top,
sitting on the crest rather than on the distal slope, and record the horizon and
the snow cover.

## Beryllium-10 exposure ages

Beryllium-10 is the workhorse nuclide for quartz-rich boulders at these
latitudes, and its production rate is calibrated against surfaces of known age.
An exposure age near the last glacial maximum places the moraine at the retreat
of the ice sheet; a cluster of ages five thousand years younger marks a
neoglacial readvance, and a single outlier usually means the boulder rolled.

Quartz is separated in the laboratory and the concentration is measured by
accelerator mass spectrometry. The age follows from the production rate, the
scaling scheme for latitude and altitude, and the erosion assumption; a change in
any of the three shifts the whole moraine by centuries, so the ages are always
published with all three stated. A boulder that rolled after deposition carries
an inherited signal or a reset clock, which is why the sampling protocol insists
on flat tops and on crest positions, and why the spread of the batch is reported
next to the mean.
